title: Pros & Cons of Money Market Mutual Funds for Emergency Savings
description: Why 'Liquid Funds' are often superior to savings accounts for high-yield cash.
content:
When you deposit cash at a bank, the bank lends it out and keeps the profit, giving you crumbs (0.01%). When you buy a **Money Market Mutual Fund (MMF)** at a brokerage, you are bypassing the bank and lending directly to the US Government or top corporations. As a result, MMFs typically yield 0.50% to 1.00% higher than the average High-Yield Savings Account. In 2025, funds like Vanguard's VMFXX or Fidelity's SPAXX have become the default 'Savings Account' for savvy investors. This guide explains the risks and rewards of ditching the bank.

Key Takeaways

  • Higher Yields: MMFs track the Fed Funds Rate closely. They often pay ~5.3% when banks pay ~4.3%. The 'middleman' spread goes to you.
  • SIPC vs. FDIC: MMFs are securities, protected by SIPC (against fraud/bankruptcy of broker). They are NOT FDIC insured against loss of value, though 'Breaking the Buck' is incredibly rare.
  • Tax Efficiency: 'Treasury' Money Market Funds (like VUSXX) are exempt from state income tax. For residents of CA/NY, this boosts the effective yield significantly.
  • Liquidity: You can usually sell and transfer cash in 1 business day. Some brokers offer check-writing directly against the fund.

Why It Matters (US Context)

In the US, Money Market Funds are regulated under Rule 2a-7 of the Investment Company Act. Reforms after 2008 made them safer, requiring higher quality assets. They are considered 'Cash Equivalents' on corporate balance sheets.

Bank vs. Brokerage

Where should your $20,000 Emergency Fund live?

Option A: Online Bank (HYSA)

  • Yield: ~4.25%.
  • Safety: FDIC Insured (Government Guarantee).
  • Ease: Simple app. Instant transfers.

Option B: Money Market Fund (MMF)

  • Yield: ~5.00% - 5.30%.
  • Safety: Backed by US Treasuries (Very Safe), but technically an investment product.
  • Ease: Lives in your brokerage account. One login for stocks + cash.
  • State Tax: Can be tax-free (if buying Treasury version).

The Math: On $20,000, the MMF earns ~$150/year more than the HYSA. If you live in California, the tax savings adds another ~$100.

How to Buy

  1. Open Brokerage: Fidelity, Vanguard, or Schwab.
  2. Choose the Core: Fidelity allows you to set SPAXX (Govt MMF) as your 'Core Position'. Any cash deposited automatically earns 5%. You don't even have to place a trade.
  3. The Tax-Free Upgrade: If in a high-tax state, manually buy the 'Treasury Only' version (e.g., FDLXX or VUSXX). Check the percentage of 'US Government Obligations' to confirm tax status.
  4. Checks and Debit: Order checks for your brokerage account. You can write a check directly against your Money Market balance. It functions like a checking account with 5% interest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I lose money?

It is theoretically possible ('Breaking the Buck' - share price drops below $1.00). It happened in 2008 to one fund. Since then, regulations are tighter. US Govt MMFs are considered risk-free by most pros.

Is there a lock-up?

No. It is daily liquidity. You can sell today and wire cash tomorrow.

Why doesn't everyone do this?

Inertia. People are used to banks. Also, during low-interest periods (2010-2020), MMFs paid 0%, so nobody cared. In high-rate environments, they are superior.
